Concave means curved inward, like the hollow of a bowl. When a surface or shape is concave, it dips inward rather than bulging outward. Picture holding a bowl right-side up — the inside surface you see is concave. It curves inward, toward a center point.
The word itself hides the clue. Look at con-cave. A cave is a hollow that cuts inward into rock. Concave works the same way — it always describes a surface or shape that curves inward, like a cave.

These two words are almost always learned as a pair because they are exact opposites. Convex means curved outward — like a dome or the outside of a ball, pushing toward you. Concave means curved inward — like the inside of that same ball.

A spoon makes this crystal clear. Flip it face-up and look at the hollow side that holds soup — that is concave. Now flip it over and look at the rounded back that bulges outward — that is convex.

You encounter concave shapes constantly. The inside of a bowl, a cup, or a spoon is concave. A satellite dish curves inward to face the sky. A contact lens is concave on the side that rests against your eyeball. A valley in a landscape dips downward in a concave shape. The inside of a skateboard half-pipe is concave. Even sunken or hollow cheeks on a person are sometimes described as concave.

In geometry, "concave" describes both curves and flat shapes (polygons).

A concave curve bends inward — like the inner edge of a circular arc that curves toward you rather than away from you.

A concave polygon is a flat, closed shape that has at least one inward-pointing "dent." A star shape is a good example — between each outward point of the star, the edges push inward. Those inward corners make it concave. More precisely, a concave polygon has at least one interior angle greater than 180 degrees. There is also a reliable visual test: if you can draw a straight line between any two points on the edge of the shape and that line passes outside the shape, the polygon is concave.

This is where the word appears most often in science, applied to lenses and mirrors.

A concave lens is thinner in the middle than at its edges. Light passing through a concave lens spreads outward, causing the light rays to diverge. This makes things appear smaller. Concave lenses are used in eyeglasses to help people who are nearsighted — people who can see things up close clearly, but struggle to see things far away.

A concave mirror curves inward, like the inside of a bowl. When light hits a concave mirror, it does not scatter — it gets reflected back and focused to a single point called the focal point. This focusing power is extremely useful. Satellite dishes use a concave shape to gather weak signals from space and direct them all to one receiver point. Telescopes use concave mirrors to collect faint starlight from the sky. Car headlights and flashlights use concave reflectors behind the bulb to aim the light forward in a tight, concentrated beam. Makeup and shaving mirrors are slightly concave — they magnify your face because they reflect light in a way that makes the image appear larger and closer than it really is.

"The architect designed a concave roof that curved inward like a bowl." "She used a concave mirror to get a magnified view while applying makeup." "The concave lens in his glasses corrects his nearsightedness." "The canyon formed a vast, concave depression in the earth." "Years of illness had left her cheeks looking hollow and concave."
The single idea that carries you everywhere

No matter what context you encounter "concave" in — science, geometry, architecture, or everyday language — it always means the same thing: curves inward. Whenever you are unsure, just ask yourself: "Does this surface curve inward, into itself?" If yes, it is concave.
